name: cpmtools
desc: Tools to access CP/M file systems
why: Reads and writes CP/M disk images from another era; a genuine doorway into old file systems and retro disk formats.

brief.what_it_is: Cpmtools is a set of command-line programs for reading and writing CP/M file system images, which are disk images from the CP/M era of 8-bit computers. It includes cpmls to list directories, cpmcp to copy files to and from a CP/M file system, cpmrm to erase files, cpmchmod and cpmchattr to change permissions and attributes, mkfs.cpm to create a new file system, fsck.cpm to check and repair one, and fsed.cpm to view one. The page describes the current release as version 2.23.
brief.why_it_exists: The author uses it for file exchange with a Z80-PC simulator, and the package is modelled on mtools, which does the same job for MS-DOS file systems. The page says it also works on floppy devices.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says the package should compile and work out of the box on any POSIX-compliant system. The source is distributed as a gzipped tar archive. The page gives no package-manager instructions, runtime requirements, or first-run steps.
brief.standout: It treats CP/M file systems the way mtools treats MS-DOS ones, so old disk images can be handled from a modern shell without an emulator's guest OS. Password protection is deliberately ignored, but a pseudo-file [passwd] exposes the stored passwords, and the disk label appears as a pseudo-file [label].
brief.status: Unknown. The page gives version 2.23 but no release date, last-commit date, or changelog, so I cannot judge how actively it is maintained.
brief.caveats: fsck.cpm only repairs simple errors so far, according to the page. Password protection is ignored rather than enforced. The page gives no license and no platform list beyond POSIX. I did not follow the linked manual pages or the source archive, so command usage and flags are not verified here.
quotes: This package allows to access CP/M file systems similar to the well-known mtools package, which accesses MSDOS file systems.
Password protection is ignored, because passwords are easy to decrypt, but a pseudo file [passwd] contains them, if you are curious what your old password has been.
Cpmtools should compile and work out of the box on each POSIX compliant system.
fetch_log: https://www.moria.de/~michael/cpmtools/ - fetched OK; page returned the project description, tool list, and version 2.23. Manual pages and source archive are mentioned but their URLs were not in the returned text, so I did not follow them.
